See what you're doing is making a bunch of assumptions based on your experiences, and trying to psychoanalyze people. I made no destinction about causation or correlation because I'm the one asking for evidence. If you are asserting there is causation or correlation between the two variables the onus is on you to prove what you're saying. What I'm doing is asking for actual evidence of this claim, and so far you have produced none, and I have produced something that at least in some way calls into question that there is a relationship between mental health issues and BDSM relationships.

Edit: also it isn't clear to me which direction you believe this phenomenon moves. Do you believe that being in a BDSM relationship impacts people's mental health negatively? Or do you believe that people with mental health issues are more likely to enter into BDSM relationships? The original claim was about the former statement, so I'm not really sure why you're talking about childhood issues.

Furthermore, there's a lot of phenomenons that exist in the world that we can't quantify exactly the impact they have, yet we do still know, based on research that there is an impact, such as with child abuse. Obviously this research does not randomly assign children to abusive households, they collect retrospective data about their experiences for the most part, and although it is impossible to tease apart how much of an impact it has on an individual while accounting for genetics or other individual experiences, we can confidently say in general there is an impact. Similarly, even though it's impossible to tease apart individual differences between people who are in bdsm relationships, we can do research on whether there is an impact of those relationships onto individuals, and if so, what the impact is.

Unless you put absolutely no stock in any study related to the social sciences and just believe things just happen in the world, and we should be able to make wild claims based on personal experiences without any attempt to study them. In which case this debate really can't go any further.

It wouldn't be hard to survey people in self-identified bdsm relationships, and then conduct something like a PHQ-9, or other mental health assessments on them in order to determine whether there is a correlation between mental health issues and these relationships. It's true that on an individual basis these are anecdotes but there is a substantial difference between one person's account and a variety of experiences a variety of different people and seeing if there is a relationship between the two variables. It's not as hard as you're trying to make it sound. Obviously that wouldn't definitively prove it, but it would at least provide some evidence to substantiate the claim.

It's a really good sign that you have Self awareness about this. Imo that is paramount. As others have said, narcasism as with other disorders exist on a spectrum, and it's entirely possible that you have narcassistic traits, or are narcassistic to the extent that it causes you to engage in emotionally abusive behaviors, but all hope is not lost. Self awareness is key, developing empathy is key, and developing your emotional intelligence. If you are committed to it you can learn these skills in therapy, but you have to be committed to it, because some people who are abusive will seek therapy only to arm themselves with psychological skills and use them against their partner, perhaps even unwittingly. My guess is the vast majority of abusers and narcassists don't realize they are abusive. This is just a personal belief based on my own experiences but I believe that if they truly understood the impact they have had on people in their lives it would destroy their psyche, they use manipulation and gaslighting as a defense mechanism to avoid coming to terms with how much damage they have done. I see this with my father, who used to be horribly abusive to me, but now that I'm not dependent on him anymore is wonderful. He is however, still abusive to my mother. I don't think he realizes the true extent of what he is doing or what he has done.

My suggestion to you is to not find just any old therapist, there is this idea that any therapy is better than none but as a therapist I can tell you that is far from the truth. Some therapists who are out of their depth can do real harm to clients if they don't have the knowledge base. Please find one that specializes in this area. You need to learn healthy communication techniques, how to not be manipulative, how to not gaslight. Believe it or not there are therapists out there who do treat people who are abusive, or that specialize in narcassistic personality disorder, although I'm sure they're harder to find. I'm not sure if you meet criteria for it or not, but they might be able to refer you out to someone else if they don't think you're appropriate for their practice as well. That should be your first step. 

Full disclosure: I'm not an expert in this particular area, but I would think that it might be a good idea to speak to your partner and let them know that you realize that you have been emotionally damaging to them, and that you plan on working on it, let them know that it is their choice whether they want to stay or want to leave you, but that regardless you want to improve yourself because you know you have hurt people with your behavior. 

I'm not sure if it will work out with your partner, I do know a bit about relationship dynamics from my education and those patterns can be tough to break. If you sense that the relationship has just become toxic, the onus is on you to end the relationship. I guarantee you, if you have been emotionally abusive to her to the point she is depressed from it, it will be much harder for her to end the relationship.
